Pronghorn calves enter the world at a neonatal body mass averaging 3000 grams [Wwb = 3000 grams], a value that reflects the species' precocial developmental strategy. This substantial birth weight enables fawns to stand and follow their mothers within hours of parturition, an adaptation to the open grassland habitats where concealment from predators is limited. Under typical thermoregulatory conditions for this species, corresponding to a core body temperature of approximately 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], females experience a gestation period of 235 days [tg = 235 days]. This relatively extended gestation, compared to other artiodactyls of similar adult size, likely facilitates the advanced state of motor and sensory development observed in neonates. Field studies in Wyoming and Montana have consistently documented birth masses clustering tightly around this value, with minimal variation observed across years, suggesting strong stabilizing selection acting on neonatal mass. The energetic demands placed on the pregnant female during this 235-day window are considerable, as she must support the rapid foetal growth that yields a calf representing roughly seven percent of her own adult mass.

Weaning represents a critical nutritional transition for the developing calf, occurring at 91 days after birth [tx = 91 days after birth] under the typical thermal conditions of this species (39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C]). At this point, the weanling has accumulated a wet body mass of 8900 grams [Wwx = 8900 grams], reflecting the substantial gains achieved during the suckling period. This mass at weaning is nearly three times the birth weight, indicating a period of rapid and efficient growth supported by the female's nutrient-rich milk, which is exceptionally high in fat content compared to many other ruminants. The timing of weaning coincides with the peak abundance of high-quality forage in late summer, allowing the now nutritionally independent juvenile to exploit readily available herbaceous vegetation. After the cessation of lactation, the young pronghorn must rely entirely on its own foraging success to continue its growth trajectory, a challenge compounded by the approaching winter months. These data on weaning mass and age were gathered from marked individuals in the National Elk Refuge and surrounding areas.

Sexual maturation in pronghorn proceeds at a measured pace, with both females and males attaining puberty at approximately 547 days from birth [tp = approximately 547 days from birth], using a core body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C] as the representative physiological baseline. This age at puberty is noteworthy among North American ungulates; for instance, it contrasts with the earlier maturation observed in white-tailed deer, which may breed as yearlings. Female pronghorn typically do not breed in their first autumn, reaching oestrus for the first time at an age of roughly eighteen months, which corresponds closely to this 547-day estimate. Males, meanwhile, undergo testicular development and the onset of spermatogenesis over a similar timeframe, though behavioural dominance in breeding herds is not achieved until several years later. The delay in reproductive maturity relative to body size likely reflects the species' relatively slow life-history pace, which is further demonstrated by the ultimate adult body masses attained. Adult females achieve an ultimate body mass of approximately 45000 grams [Wwi = approximately 45000 grams], though this value can range from 34 to 48 kilograms depending on habitat quality and regional forage availability.

The maximum lifespan recorded for pronghorn under natural conditions, measured at the species' typical core body temperature of 39.5 °C [T = 39.5 °C], extends to approximately 15.5 years [am = approximately 15.5 years]. This longevity is substantial for a medium-sized ungulate and is comparable to that of larger bovids such as bison, despite the pronghorn's smaller body size. Males attain a larger asymptotic body mass than females, with the ultimate wet weight for males reaching as high as 60000 grams [Wwi = 60000 grams], a figure that falls within the documented range of 40 to 65 kilograms for prime-aged individuals. The species' long lifespan is coupled with a conservative reproductive strategy; females produce just one litter per year [F_R_i = one litter per year], with each litter typically containing two calves [N_R_i = each litter typically containing two calves]. Annual reproductive output is therefore modest, capped at a maximum of two offspring per female each breeding season. This combination of extended longevity, moderate body size, and low fecundity aligns pronghorn with a slow life-history syndrome typically associated with species inhabiting stable, predictable environments where adult survival is prioritised over high reproductive output.

Among females, the mass range spans from 34 to 48 kilograms, encompassing variation across the species' geographic distribution, from the shortgrass prairies of the Great Plains to the sagebrush steppe of the Intermountain West. The female's body composition undergoes dramatic seasonal shifts, with maximal mass achieved just before parturition and minimal mass occurring during the late winter period of nutritional stress. Males, which attain masses between 40 and 65 kilograms, exhibit a similarly large range, with peak condition observed at the onset of the autumn breeding season when rutting males weigh the most. The calving season itself is tightly synchronized, with the vast majority of births occurring over a two-to-three-week window in late spring, a phenological adaptation that matches the period of highest neonatal survival to the flush of green vegetation.
